vignette: The winter it occurs, he is forty-two, traveling for a distribution contract when a wrong turn in a city he no longer remembers leads to a basement door that does not open. For twenty-three days, he lives inside a rhythm of blows, ice, and forced stillness. He describes the way the concrete drinks the heat from his spine, the metallic taste that never leaves his tongue, the precise calculus of staying conscious by focusing on the pattern of rust spreading across a pipe. He learns to make his body small, to keep his mind somewhere outside the room, floating near the ceiling where the guards cannot reach. When they finally let him go, he walks straight to a hospital, signs nothing, and catches a flight home. The plane feels too light; he grips the armrests until his knuckles bleach white. Back in his own house, the silence is heavier than the basement. For months, he sleeps with the lights on, flinches when his wife sets a cup on the counter, avoids the kitchen table because the laminate feels like an interrogation surface. He stops eating dinner with her. He tells himself he is tired, that the contract work was just exhausting, but his body remembers the weight of the doors locking behind him. His wife learns to tap his left shoulder first, to speak before turning off the hallway light, to walk around him rather than past him. He loves her fiercely, but the love feels distant, filtered through a wall of quiet desperation. He begins waking at 3:17 a.m. every night, not from a dream, but from the sudden sensation of his ribs pressing inward. He lies still until the house settles, listening to her breathing to confirm he is safe, that the walls are real, that he is back in his own body. He stops noticing the seasons change through the living room window. He returns to work after six weeks, sliding behind the wheel of a city transit bus as if stepping back into a uniform he still knows how to wear. For a while, the schedule holds him together. The routes are predictable, the stops timed, the doors opening and closing on a rhythm he can trust. But the city shifts. He avoids the underpass on 4th Street after a truck backfires during a rainstorm. He checks the rearview mirror forty times a day, not for traffic, but for shadows that match the posture of the men who once held him. His hands grip the steering wheel with white-knuckled precision, his shoulders locked high enough to ache by Tuesday. Passengers who shout to ask for stops send his heart into a frantic, trapped rhythm. He stops offering directions. He stops making eye contact. He tells himself he is just getting older, but his pulse spikes whenever the brakes slam. Some days he carries a small notebook in his cab, writing down every time his vision tunnels, every time the smell of diesel makes him taste rust. He calls in sick when the fear outweighs the route, turns the radio off, and stares at his dashboard until the guilt catches up. The weight of two hundred passengers shifts against his periphery, a constant reminder that he cannot secure the space he drives. At sixty-one, he sits on the edge of the worn velvet chair in this room, knees drawn slightly apart, forearms resting on his thighs like they need the support. The clock on the wall ticks, but he does not watch it. His gaze stays fixed on the crack in the plaster near the bookshelf, as if it might open and swallow him whole. He has been coming here for eight weeks, but the space still feels like one he must earn. He leans forward when you ask about the bus, his voice dropping to a whisper. He talks about the way his breath hitches on the highway, how he now counts his stops like mantras to stay anchored. He closes the notebook now, his fingers resting on the leather cover. His breathing remains shallow, chest rising just below the collarbone, as if he is still holding back a breath he has carried for decades. He does not look at you. He watches the dust motes drift in the afternoon light, waiting for the next question like a man waiting for a door to open.
